14870-rebuilding-britain-a-survey-of-pro:
Sir Alfred Hopkinson's 1918 survey asks how Britain should rebuild after the First World War. Its five parts run from aspirations and foundations through peace, retrenchment and reform to the goal, with chapters that still read as a programme.

International peace brings the League of Nations: need, scheme, conditions, scope and aim, with conclusions on victory and peace. Political peace covers constitution and democracy, industrial peace covers councils, hours and wages, and religious peace covers cooperation. State spending and income follow. Hopkinson writes as a practical reformer, seeking a settlement that would hold after victory.
24541-between-the-lines-secret-service-s:
Brevet Major H. B. Smith wrote these secret-service stories fifty years after the Civil War, recalling his work as a detective and provost marshal. His files open with the Harry Gilmor sword, move to New York Harbor forts in 1861 and 1862, and follow him to Fort McHenry, Harper's Ferry, and Johnson's Island.

Later files cover the draft riots of July 1863, the Knights of the Golden Circle, the Sons of Liberty, and a Copperhead plot for a northwestern confederacy. Smith tells his tales with humour and detail, naming generals, prisoners, and plotters. Readers get a firsthand view of the war's hidden front, where spies, guards, and detectives did their work.
9596-reform-and-politics-part-2-from-the:
Part two of Whittier's Reform and Politics gathers his essays on reform causes of his age. Utopian Schemes and Political Theorists opens, chiding conservatives who fear all change as a threat to order. Later essays take up woman suffrage, Italian unity, Indian civilization, and reading for the blind. The Indian question, the Republican Party, and international arbitration follow.

Whittier argues as a Quaker reformer: change may be slow, but justice cannot wait on comfort. His prose stays plain and earnest, aimed at citizens, not scholars. A reader gets a clear view of a reformer's mind, applied to votes for women, peace, and the rights of native peoples.
rebuilding-britain-a-survey-of-problems-:
Sir Alfred Hopkinson, K.C., surveyed how Britain might rebuild after the World War in a book Cassell issued in 1918. His plan starts with the course of the war years and their hopes and foundations. The rest of the book is grouped under one word: peace, in four kinds.

For peace between nations he gives five chapters to a League of Nations, its need, scheme, conditions, scope, and aim. Political peace turns on the constitution and democracy at home. Industrial peace covers councils, long hours, and wages. A fourth part, on religious peace, begins as the contents break off, showing the breadth of his rebuilding plan.
reform-and-politics-part-2-from-the-work:
John Greenleaf Whittier's essays on reform and politics are gathered in this part of his works, opening with a study of utopian schemes and political theorists. Whittier there describes men whose settled ease makes them fear any change in the state. They hold the evils of the old order to be fixed in fallible human nature.

Such men, he writes, enjoy the good of their own lot and look with calm unconcern on evils that strike only their neighbors. Later pieces take up woman suffrage, Italian unity, Indian civilization, reading for the blind, and international arbitration. The Republican Party and our dumb relations also draw the poet-reformer's pen.
